title: 防災工学Ⅱ
subtitle: Disaster Prevention Engineering II
educationalGoal:
This course aims to provide a basic knowledge of present seismic design methods,  and learn the mechanism of each disaster, such as earthquake, slope failure or debris flow at short time heavy rain, in relationship with geology and geomorphology.
Students will recognize and understand both hard and soft countermeasures to prevent or mitigate against the disasters.
advice:
Earthquake
1. Mechanism of earthquake around Japan.
2. Comparison of seismic indexes and relationship with damages.
3. Seismic design in national highway design book.
4. Simple estimation method for liquefaction

Slope Sliding in heavy rain
Countermeasure and mitigation in disasters
Other types of disasters (Volcano, Heavy snow)
Urban disaster prevention and Hazard Mapping
Disaster recordings
requiredKnowledge: Knowledge of Soil Mechanics I and II, Basic knowledge and interest in disaster are also needed.

activityGoals.body: be able to understand the mechanism, relationship between seismic wave and damages.
be able to understand seismic coefficient design method.
be able to understand the mechanism of liquefaction, slope sliding, also law related issues in Japan.
be able to understand fundamental idea of disaster prevention/mitigation, from both hard and soft point of view.

achievementLevels.ideal:
(1) Fully understand the behavioral goals of Disaster Prevention Engineering II, and acquire basic skills as an civil engineer.
(2) Understand design concept of present national criterion and its problem.
(3) be able to propose an effective countermeasure or mitigation plan against disasters.
achievementLevels.standard:
(1) Understand the behavioral goals of Disaster Prevention Engineering II, the basic design concept of seismic coefficient method and simple estimation method of liquefaction, as civil engineer.
(2) Understand the cause of disaster damages and recognize those importance
(3) Be able to use the obtaining knowledge for its action or selection of future profession.
